title: Living ashtpadi 22
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, rijak, and your line: he feeds all. A week ends today: before creation, the play beginning, the quiet behind all things, the Lord of all, every heart, and the One who feeds every creature.

Sikhs tell a story about the seventh Guru, Guru Har Rai, when he was a boy. Walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe, he brushed past a flowering bush, and a few petals fell to the ground. His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it and told him gently that a robe that wide must be carried with care. The boy, the story goes, was so moved that he kept that care all his life.
screen: `A BOY, A ROBE, A FLOWERING BUSH.` → `A FEW PETALS FALL.` → `CARRY IT WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-second ashtpadi in brief. God is the thaakur, the Master, of jeea jant, every living being. The One is spread through them all, dwelling ghat ghat, in every heart, and sustaining each creature with its daily bread. Put together, one plain line: everything alive is His. Living it starts with how we touch things. The story of Guru Har Rai is passed down in Sikh tradition rather than recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, but its point fits the ashtpadi exactly. If every living thing belongs to the One, a flower isn't just scenery and an animal isn't just a resource. They're in someone else's care, and we're walking through the garden. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai as a lover of gardens and animals, and as someone who kept medicines to give to the sick, including, by many accounts, the son of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose family were no friends of the Gurus. That detail matters. Everything alive is His, including the people we'd rather not help. In practice, this can be very small: watering the office plant everyone forgets, driving a little slower past the park, asking how the elderly neighbor's dog is doing. None of it is grand. But each small act says: this life isn't mine to waste. It belongs to the One who is spread through all.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: MASTER, PRESENT, FEEDER.` · `A STORY PEOPLE TELL.` · `MEDICINE FOR AN ENEMY'S SON.` · `SMALL ACTS OF CARE.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING ALIVE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was food; today is care. Tend one living thing slowly, a plant that needs water, litter on the path outside, a tired person at home who'd like a cup of tea, as if it belonged to someone you love, because in the ashtpadi's picture it does; or, if nothing is nearby, picture the one you'll care for later. If you pray, say Waheguru as you tend it.
Jeea, living beings, those with life and breath: every jeea has the same Master, the same indwelling Light, the same Feeder; so every living thing is handled with care.
Your line: everything alive is his. Seven days, from the stillness to the garden. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: It's just a flower. Why would a Guru care about a few fallen petals?
options: In the ashtpadi everything alive is God's, so even a flower is in someone else's care.
The story says flowers are sacred, so picking one is a sin that can't be forgiven.
The story is about neatness: a Guru's robe should always look tidy and clean.
chat.meaning: The ashtpadi says the One is Master of every living being, so a flower isn't just scenery: it's in God's care, and we're walking through the garden.

Guru Hargobind.meaning: the sixth Guru, Guru Har Rai's grandfather
